title: The geography & economy of Punjab's long drug crisis
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages of organised crime with terrorism; Security challenges in border areas; Role of external state and non-state actors · GS2 › Issues relating to health; Government policies and interventions · GS1 › Social issues: youth, women · GS4 › Probity in governance
summary: An anti-drug activist's killing and a recent overdose death have put Punjab's 15-year drug crisis back at the centre of politics ahead of next year's Assembly elections.
ideas: Geography makes Punjab vulnerable: its 553-km border with Pakistan lies on the route from the Golden Crescent (Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran). Police officers call Pakistan's pushing of drugs into Punjab after militancy faded 'narco-terrorism'.
GS3 · Border security / narco-terrorism
Punjab's 553-km border with Pakistan places it on the Golden Crescent route, turning drug trafficking into a security threat.

Supply from all directions: heroin (chitta) comes across the border, opium and poppy husk from Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh (where cultivation is legal for medical use), charas from Himachal Pradesh, and pharmaceutical drugs from manufacturing hubs in neighbouring states.
GS3 · Organised crime · GS2 · Centre-state coordination
Drugs reach Punjab from across the border and from neighbouring states, so the fight needs coordination among states, not only border policing.

The problem shifts when pressed: as border enforcement improved, abuse of pharmaceutical drugs rose sharply, and smugglers turned to drones, mostly small Chinese quadcopters dropping heroin and arms, often in daylight.
GS3 · Technology and security
Each crackdown has shifted the trade to a new route, from heroin to pharma drugs and from land to drones.

Social and economic roots: opium had social acceptance even before Independence; a single run as a drug mule can earn about a lakh where jobs lag aspirations; easy, underhand wealth is increasingly accepted; whole families, including women, are drawn in.
GS1 · Youth / women · GS3 · Unemployment
Unemployment and social acceptance of easy money feed both addiction and the trade, making it a social as much as a security problem.

Enforcement first, prevention later: governments have followed the EDP model (Enforcement, De-addiction, Prevention), from a 'war on drugs' (2014) and supply crackdowns (2022) to Yudh Nasheyan Virudh (2025), which targeted drug money and moved to community action with 1.5 lakh village volunteers. Drugs remain available; observers say prevention and rehabilitation should come first.
GS2 · Government interventions / health
Enforcement alone has not ended Punjab's drug crisis; prevention and rehabilitation must lead, with enforcement in support.
keywords: Golden Crescent
Pakistan, Afghanistan and Iran: one of the world's three major heroin-processing hubs
GS3 · Border security
Punjab's western border sits on the Golden Crescent route, making it India's frontline against heroin.
Golden Triangle
Myanmar, Thailand and Laos: the other major heroin-producing region near India
GS3 · North-East security
India lies between the Golden Crescent in the west and the Golden Triangle in the east.
Narco-terrorism
Using drugs to weaken a state or fund terror
GS3 · Internal security
Drug trafficking across Punjab's border is a form of narco-terrorism, not just crime.
Balloon effect
Pressing one supply route pushes the trade to another
GS3 · Enforcement
The shift from border heroin to pharma drugs shows the balloon effect of supply-only enforcement.
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs
Medicines leaking from legal supply into addiction
GS2 · Health regulation
Diversion of pharmaceutical drugs calls for tighter regulation of manufacturers and chemists.
Supply-side vs demand-side approach
Policing the trade versus reducing the need for drugs
GS2 · Policy
A lasting answer must balance supply-side policing with demand-side prevention and rehabilitation.
Financial investigation
Targeting traffickers' money and assets
GS3 · Money laundering
Following the money hurts trafficking networks more than arresting carriers.
Community policing
Involving local people in enforcement and prevention
GS3 · Policing
Village volunteers make the anti-drug effort a community movement, not just a police drive.
data: Cases of drug possession for trafficking in Punjab in 2024, the highest in India (Uttar Pradesh next with 3,219)
Punjab recorded 6,060 drug-trafficking possession cases in 2024, the highest in India (NCRB).
Share of India's pharmaceutical drug seizures / heroin seizures in Punjab alone, 2024
Punjab alone accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures and 44% of heroin seizures in 2024.

Drone drops on the Punjab border rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025 (BSF).
Rise in arrests of women under the NDPS Act, 2015 to 2022
Arrests of women under the NDPS Act in Punjab rose 85% between 2015 and 2022.
Extension of BSF jurisdiction inland in Punjab, 2021
In 2021 the Centre extended the BSF's jurisdiction from 15 km to 50 km inland.
examples: Drone belt: Amritsar–Tarn Taran–Ferozepur–Gurdaspur
The BSF set up an anti-drone intelligence wing and Punjab Police bought anti-drone guns, yet smugglers still evade them
GS3 · Technology and security
Despite anti-drone units, drones still ferry drugs and arms across the Punjab border.
The 2013 Bhola case
A Punjab Police DSP arrested in a multimillion-rupee drug racket, convicted in 2019
GS4
GS3 · Crime nexus · GS4 · Probity
The Bhola case exposes the nexus of traffickers, police and politicians that sustains the drug trade.
Women as carriers
Traffickers use women because they are less likely to be searched; some women addicts turn peddlers
GS1 · Women / organised crime
Traffickers exploit women as carriers, adding a gender dimension to the drug trade.
1.5 lakh village volunteers
Community-driven phase of Punjab's anti-drug campaign
GS2 · People's participation
Punjab's 1.5 lakh village volunteers show community participation as part of the fight against drugs.
pyqs: The Golden Crescent next door and the links between drugs, arms and money: the Punjab border is the live case.
Drones ferrying arms and drugs: drone drops rose from 3 (2021) to over 200 (2025).
Narco-terrorism: Pakistan pushing drugs into Punjab after militancy faded.

trend.t: UPSC moved from the links between drug trafficking and other crimes (2018) to the technology that carries drugs, drones (2023), and then to narco-terrorism as a national threat (2024). GS4 also set a case study on a frontier district overrun by narcotics (2019).
trend.watch: Drugs and security have come in GS3 in 2018, 2023 and 2024, and in a GS4 case study in 2019. Narco-terrorism is a must-study area.

answer.t: Punjab accounted for about 57% of India's pharma drug seizures in 2024, and BSF-recorded drone drops rose from 3 in 2021 to over 200 in 2025.

pts.t: Pressure on one route pushes the trade to another, so supply-only enforcement keeps chasing the problem.
pts.ex: Heroin to pharma drugs after border tightening.

pts.t: Pharma drugs come from licensed manufacturers and chemists, making them harder to police than contraband.
pts.ex: About 80% enter Punjab from hubs in neighbouring states.

pts.t: Supply comes from several states, but policing is state-wise, leaving coordination gaps.
Small quadcopters drop drugs and arms, often in daylight, and evade detection.
The same drones carry arms, tying drug smuggling to terrorism.
Collusion between traffickers, police and politicians weakens enforcement.
Track sales of habit-forming medicines from manufacturer to chemist.
Layered detection and jamming along the border, with BSF–state police coordination.
Financial investigation to break trafficking networks.
De-addiction, rehabilitation and jobs for youth, with community participation.

answer.t: Only a strategy that cuts both supply and demand can break a trade that adapts faster than enforcement.

title: For affordable cancer care, go beyond price caps
syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to development and management of health; Government policies and interventions · GS3 › Issues relating to intellectual property rights · GS4 › Ethics in business
summary: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP; the editorial argues the cap alone will not make treatment affordable.
ideas: The cap tackles only the middlemen: it limits the margin on sale to patients, not the price at which companies sell to distributors or hospitals. If that starting price is high, the drug stays unaffordable.
GS2 · Health / regulation
Capping trade margins treats the symptom downstream while the real cost is set upstream by the manufacturer's price.
Patents give pricing power: patented cancer drugs face little generic competition, so manufacturers control prices, and earlier caps on the same drugs did not stop prices from rising.
GS3 · IPR and access to medicines
Where patents shut out generics, price caps on margins cannot discipline the manufacturer's price.
Hidden discounts hide the real price: steep discounts on a few units to select corporate hospitals, with most stock sold higher, make the true market price hard for regulators to know.
GS2 · Regulatory capacity
Selective discounts distort the market price, so margin regulation needs scrutiny of manufacturers' prices and transparent sales data.
A blanket cap can backfire: pharmacies have genuine storage and handling costs; a rigid cap could disrupt supplies to underserved areas, and hospitals may pass costs on through higher room rents.
GS2 · Policy design
A blanket price cap risks shortages in underserved areas and cost-shifting by hospitals.
Price control works only with the health system: stronger public health services, wider insurance coverage and more research on generics must accompany the cap.
GS2 · Universal health coverage
Affordable cancer care needs price regulation backed by public health services, insurance and generics.

GS3 · IPR

Limits of the public health system and the private sector's role: affordable medicines are part of universal coverage.
Section 3(d) and the Novartis case: patents versus access to affordable medicines.

trend.t: Health questions moved from goals and access (MDGs 2013, universal coverage 2015, community-level care 2018) to the State's moral and practical role (primary health 2021) and, most recently, to containing the marketisation of healthcare (2024). In GS3, patents and access to medicines appeared in 2013.
trend.watch: The balance between the State and the private sector in health has come in 2015 and 2024. Regulation of the health market is a must-study area.
focus: State regulation of drug prices and hospital charges

answer.t: The government has capped the seller's profit on non-scheduled cancer drugs at 30% of the MRP, where intermediaries added an average 170% mark-up (NPPA).

pts.t: Margin caps do not cover the manufacturer's price to distributors and hospitals.
pts.ex: Ribociclib's cost rose from ₹58,000 to ₹78,000 despite 2019 caps.

pts.t: Patented drugs face little generic competition, so prices stay high.
Selective discounts to corporate hospitals hide the real market price.
Hospitals may recover capped margins through room rents and other charges.
Rigid caps may make supply to underserved areas unviable for pharmacies.
Low insurance coverage leaves patients paying out of pocket.
pts.ex: Patients delay treatment or skip doses.

pts.t: Mandatory reporting of sales and discounts.
More research on and production of generic versions.
Strengthen public hospitals and coverage for cancer care.
Allow for legitimate storage and handling costs.

answer.t: Price caps can lower bills, but only a strong public health system can make cancer care truly affordable.

title: Clean air needs targets, timelines, accountability
syllabus: GS3 › Environmental pollution and degradation · GS2 › Government policies and interventions; Inter-ministerial coordination · GS4 › Environmental ethics; Accountability
summary: Clean-air policy rewards paperwork, not cleaner air; as India drafts NCAP 2.0, the writer wants success measured by reduced exposure, with deadlines and accountability across departments.
evolution: National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) launched for cities that fail air quality standards.
Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan ranks Lucknow India's best million-plus city, yet its PM10 is still over twice the safe standard.
CREA finds no appreciable improvement in Delhi's winter air over four years, despite GRAP.
ideas: Seasonal amnesia: toxic air returns every winter, draws outrage, then is forgotten till the next cycle.
GS3 · Air pollution (introduction)
India's response to air pollution suffers from 'seasonal amnesia': outrage every winter, forgotten by spring.

Process, not outcome: Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan scores roads swept and plans made; actual cuts in particulate matter count for just 2.5% of a city's score. This is the blind spot in India's clean-air strategy.
GS3 · Policy design / NCAP
With actual pollution reduction worth only 2.5% of a city's Swachh Vayu score, India rewards process, not cleaner air.
Delay destroys benefits: a filter installed in 2034 cannot clean the air a child breathed in 2026; the cost of delay must enter policy.
GS3 · Economics of pollution
Delay in clean air does not postpone benefits; it destroys them.

Clean air is everyone's job: pollution comes from transport, power, industry, waste, agriculture and cooking, so it cannot stay with the environment ministry alone. Institutional fragmentation slips deadlines and diffuses accountability.
GS2 · Coordination / GS3 governance
Air pollution spans transport, power, industry, farming and households, so clean air must be the collective responsibility of every department, not the environment ministry alone.
NCAP 2.0 should measure success by exposure reduced, speed of relief and who answers for missed deadlines, with central grants and Finance Commission transfers rewarding sustained cuts.
GS3 · Way forward
NCAP 2.0 must tie funds, including Finance Commission grants, to sustained cuts in people's exposure, not to activities.

pyqs: NCAP has been asked; NCAP 2.0 and its shift to outcomes is the natural follow-up.
WHO's stricter guidelines make India's national standard (PM10 of 60) look lax; even top-ranked Lucknow is over twice it.
Why Delhi's air is worst: winter inversion and regional sources; four years of GRAP have not fixed it.
Smog is the visible face of the seasonal crisis the writer calls 'seasonal amnesia'.
Clean air as part of the right to life under Article 21.
Waste management is part of clean air; city rankings reward such activities.

trend.t: Air pollution has been asked from many sides: the geography of Delhi's smog (GS1 2015), the right to clean air (GS2 2015), the NCAP programme (GS3 2020), WHO's air quality guidelines (2021) and photochemical smog (2022). The questions have moved from causes to programmes and standards.
trend.watch: Air pollution comes up every one or two years across GS1, GS2 and GS3. With NCAP already asked, NCAP 2.0 and outcome-based clean-air governance are must-study.

answer.t: Launched in 2019, NCAP has built plans and budgets for polluting cities, yet even top-ranked Lucknow has PM10 over twice the safe standard, and Delhi's winter air has not improved in four years (CREA).

pts.ex: An eight-year delay halves Delhi-NCR's 2040 exposure gain (UNEP).

pts.t: Pollution crosses municipal and state lines.
No agency answers for missed deadlines.

Tie central and Finance Commission grants to sustained exposure cuts.
Give transport, power, industry, agriculture and urban departments their own targets.
Plan across states and cities that share air.
Fix timelines and name the agency answerable for each.
pts.ex: 'Not another list of measures, but a stopwatch'.

pts.t: Use health and GDP losses to prioritise spending.
pts.ex: 10% of South Asia's GDP lost each year (UNEP); ₹21 back per ₹1 invested.

pts.t: Apply the clarity that worked in Ujjwala and solar power.

answer.t: NCAP 2.0 must judge itself by the air people breathe, with every department accountable to a clock.

title: Keralam passes India's first state law to protect senior citizens' rights
syllabus: GS2 › Welfare schemes and laws for vulnerable sections · GS1 › Population and demographic transition · GS4 › Compassion towards the weaker sections
context: The Keralam Assembly passed the Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026, the first state-level legal framework for elder welfare. It makes elder care rights-based, regulated and professional.
ideas: Elder care moves from charity and family duty to rights backed by the state.
GS2 · Vulnerable sections
Keralam's 2026 law moves elder care from charity to enforceable rights.
Ageing in place: care at home first, institutions as the last resort.
GS1 · Ageing and family
With joint families shrinking, 'ageing in place', care at home first, is the humane model.
The care economy needs standards: regulated care homes and certified caregivers.
GS2 social sector · GS3 jobs
Regulated care homes and certified caregivers can turn the care economy into decent jobs.
keywords: Rights-based approach
Welfare as an entitlement, not a favour
Any welfare answer
A rights-based approach treats welfare as an entitlement, as Keralam's elder-rights law does.
Ageing in place
Older people living independently at home
GS1 · Ageing
Keralam's law gives senior citizens the right to age in place, safely at home.
Living will
Advance written choice on life-sustaining treatment
Passive euthanasia
Keralam's law recognises living wills, extending dignity to the end of life.
Care economy
Paid and unpaid work of looking after others
Ageing / women / jobs
Ageing raises demand for the care economy, much of it unpaid work by women.
examples: Keralam Senior Citizens (Care and Protection of Rights) Bill, 2026
India's first state-level elder-rights framework
Best practice
Keralam's Senior Citizens Bill, 2026, India's first state elder-rights law, is a model for other ageing states.
pyqs: Ageing is a core challenge of the demographic transition; Keralam's law is a policy response.
As family support weakens, the state steps in with a rights framework for the aged.
The Bill recognises living wills for senior citizens, linking to the passive-euthanasia debate.
summary: Keralam passed India's first state law giving senior citizens enforceable rights: to age at home, to make living wills, and to regulated care.
evolution: Central Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act focused on maintenance by children (background, not from the report).
Keralam moves to a rights-based law covering care standards, caregivers and living wills.
